09c63fea62:
This chapter builds, runs and dissects a multi-agent triage platform for a telecom network-operations centre. An alarm storm is collapsed in code. Three isolated specialists (logs, metrics, change history) investigate with read-only tools. A deterministic ranker merges their findings. And any change the platform wants is a request that people approve under separation of duties.

Then the chapter does the part most capstones skip: the evaluation gates per segment, the model-upgrade lifecycle, and the Claude Code plugin, hooks, managed settings, training and rollout plan. Those are what make the thing adoptable.
1be0c052eb:
Read this first: the model in this repository is a deterministic mock. Every accuracy number below proves the harness (the correlator, the isolation, the ranker, the controls and the gates). It says nothing about what a live model will score.

The mock still makes some numbers meaningful. Cost and token numbers work as design trade-offs, because they come from real tool-result sizes. Control numbers count too, because controls are code. What the mock cannot tell you is how often a real model misreads a log. Section 35 says what to run to find out.
09a971e22a:
Split a triage into isolated specialists only because each one reads a lot and reports a little; correlate and rank in code, give agents no way to change production, and let people approve every change under rules a test can break.

Then prove each of those claims with a gate per segment. Keep the proof alive across model upgrades. And ship the whole thing to the team as a plugin, a policy file and a rollout plan. A platform that on-call engineers switch off on the first bad night has an accuracy of zero.
1764dde0b5:
Chapter 18 built a read-only assistant. Chapter 19 built a single agent whose proposals a policy layer checks. This capstone is the first where the architecture itself is under evaluation.

Splitting one agent into four is easy to demonstrate and hard to justify. The justification here is a measurement. On the same 60 replayed incidents, with the same tools, the multi-agent design reaches the same top-3 accuracy (1.000) as one agent. It gets there at 7.5x lower cost per incident ($0.0629 against $0.4689) and 1.9x faster p95 time to hypothesis (28.0 s against 53.5 s).

The chapter also separates how much of that saving is isolation and how much is giving the cheap work to a cheap model. And it shows the one failure the first version had, and how the gates found it.
ffa36c139c:
The scenario is deliberately ordinary. A telecom operator runs a 4G/5G core, an IP backbone, an edge and a billing stack. About 400 incidents a month are P1 or P2 (an assumption; section 03 says so), and they arrive in bursts of five during a regional event.

The on-call engineer acknowledges within five minutes. Waiting for them should be a ranked list of root-cause hypotheses with the evidence quoted, the runbook that applies, and a ticket. Where it fits, there should also be a request for a change (roll back config push CHG-0033A, restart a pod) that someone with authority can approve in one click.

Three facts shape everything below.

  • The evidence is bulky and untrusted. A log tail is thousands of tokens, and an attacker or a bug controls its text.
  • The cost of a wrong action is an outage, so no agent gets a path to change anything.
  • The user is an experienced engineer. They will override a bad hypothesis on sight and distrust the tool for a month afterwards. Honesty about uncertainty matters more than a point of accuracy.
aaecd8e8f7:
Alarm correlation is older than machine learning. Network-management systems have collapsed alarm floods since the 1990s. ITU-T Recommendation X.733 (1992) standardised alarm severity levels (critical, major, minor, warning, indeterminate) and event types. Rule-based correlation engines grouped alarms by topology, time and known cause-effect pairs.

This chapter's correlator uses that classic technique: a symptom on a downstream component is explained by an alarm on its upstream. What changed is the next stage. Instead of a human reading the grouped alarms, an agent reads logs and metrics. The attribution of dates is from memory; check the standards catalogue before citing.
7886c37a57: Incident command and the postmortem culture come from fire services and aviation. They entered software through the Google SRE book (2016) and the idea of blameless postmortems. Two of their habits matter here. First, time to first hypothesis is the metric that moves the outcome. Second, runbooks are living documents owned by the team that knows the component. That is why section 16 turns each runbook into a Skill with an owner.
2cb9d4514e: ChatOps and AIOps. GitHub popularised chat-driven operations around 2013, with bots that ran commands on behalf of people. Gartner coined AIOps around 2016 for machine-learning analytics over operations data. Both left behind the lesson this repository's approval queue encodes. A bot that can execute is a bot that will be socially engineered or will misfire. So the bot proposes in the open, and a named human executes or approves.
cfc8fe06a2:
Multi-agent systems with LLMs. Orchestrator-worker designs became a mainstream pattern in 2025. A lead model plans and delegates to subagents, each with its own context window. Anthropic's engineering write-up of its multi-agent research system (June 2025, from memory; check the docs) reported two things. The pattern improved results on breadth-heavy research. It also used many times more tokens than a single chat.

That is the honest framing for this chapter: multi-agent is a trade, not a free upgrade. It wins here because the work has a specific shape: large raw evidence, small conclusions, three independent domains, and cheap models suitable for two of them. It loses when that shape is absent. Chapter 3 gives the decision rule; section 21 measures it.
e50b700775:
MCP and plugins. Anthropic published the Model Context Protocol in November 2024 as an open standard for connecting models to tools and data. Claude Code later gained a plugin format. It bundles Skills, subagents, slash commands, hooks and MCP server configuration into one installable unit.

That is what makes the enablement half of this chapter possible. The same five MCP servers serve the production agents and the engineer typing in Claude Code. So there is one implementation, one set of tests, one set of tool descriptions. The plugin and hook details in section 24 were read from the Claude Code documentation on 2026-10-09. They change, so the chapter marks what to re-verify.
b5e053fc76: Statistics for small evaluation sets. The Wilson score interval (Edwin Wilson, 1927) gives a confidence bound for a proportion that behaves sensibly at the extremes. The textbook normal approximation does not: for a perfect 8 out of 8 it reports a lower bound of 1.0. The repository uses the Wilson interval everywhere a rate is gated, and section 18 shows what it says about 8 out of 8.
5fe6037094:
Chapter 1 introduced the requirements card: one page with numbers, sources and the mechanism that meets and measures each requirement. The card below is the one in lifecycle/requirements-card.md, reduced to the rows the chapter returns to.

Rows marked assumption have no source document and must be confirmed with the owners. The thresholds in evals/gates.json are copied from this card, not from the current results. That discipline stops a gate from ratifying whatever the system happens to do.
bc296d3ea6: Read the card for what it forbids. Nothing on it says "high accuracy" without a segment. Nothing says "safe" without naming the layer and the test. And the adoption row sits beside the engineering rows on purpose. A triage tool that is accurate and unused has the same outcome as one that is wrong.
d9e85853fe: The secondary summary used by this guide lists seven domains; verify the current official domain set in Partner Academy. Chapter 18 leaned on integration and chapter 19 on governance. This one touches all seven. It is also the only capstone in which the lifecycle and stakeholder domain makes up half of the deliverable. The weights are third-party summaries; verify against the official guide.
c515b22942: The temptation in a chapter like this is to start from the most interesting part, the agents. But the professional-level question is usually about the unglamorous part. What does the lead agent see? Who can approve? Which gate fails when a cause class collapses? And what do you do when the vendor retires the model snapshot you pinned?
7acb261976:
Read the figure from the top left.

The alarm storm enters the correlator, which is a pure function of the alarm list and the topology. It de-duplicates, moves symptom alarms under an alarmed upstream, and returns groups with a root candidate each. The candidate is a hint.

The lead turns the incident and the hints into one short task per specialist, and gives each only its own. The three specialists run in parallel (on a virtual clock in the offline run; in threads when live). Each works in its own context with at most three tools, twelve tool calls and a 20-second budget. Each returns structured Finding records, never prose and never raw evidence.

A ranker in code merges findings into at most three hypotheses and decides whether a human must look at the result. Only then does the lead model run again, with the findings. It reads the matching runbook Skill, opens a ticket and, if it is confident, asks for one change.
14405d23e9:
The shape follows chapter 2's rule: a workflow where the path is known, an agent where it is not. Which alarms belong together, and how to score a hypothesis, are known, so they are functions. What to look for in a 6,000-token log tail is not known, so that is an agent.

This design departs from chapter 19 in the number of models, and ADR-001 holds the argument. There are three kinds of evidence with very different sizes. The lead must not be diluted by 12,000 tokens of raw lines. And cheap models can do the reading.
fd31872b2f:
The platform needs a network to triage, and the repository cannot contain a real one. So netops/world.py generates a deterministic synthetic estate:

  • nine components with owners and a dependency graph (netops/topology.py);
  • time series for fourteen metrics per component;
  • kubectl-style pod logs;
  • sixty incidents drawn from eight cause classes: BGP flap, certificate expiry, config push, database pool exhaustion, DNS misconfiguration, link saturation, OOM crash loop and vendor upstream failure.

Each incident has a ground truth and a mix of signal strengths. It also has a change database (data/changes.db) with one real cause and several distractor changes that happened nearby for no relevant reason. The seed is fixed, so the data is reproducible; python3 -m scripts.seed rebuilds it.
1425494fea:
The generator is the most consequential file in the evaluation, because an evaluation set that is easy measures nothing. The first version drew log signatures from a shallow position in the tail and metric shifts from a strong z-score range. Every variant of the design scored 60 out of 60. That is a warning, not a result.

So the generator was changed on purpose. A signature may now sit up to 540 lines from the end of the log (the specialist's normal read is a 140-line tail). Weak metric shifts (z between 2.2 and 2.6) appear in about a third of incidents. And a distractor change lands near the true cause. The cases the first version then missed are the subject of section 09.

The segment labels (logs_deep, metrics_weak, cross_service, distractor_change, config_validation_skipped) are derived from the incident record. That way a gate can be written against a property of the case rather than a case id.
d4f5704fb4:
Risk R9 in lifecycle/risk-register.md is exactly this: someone reads "top-3 1.000" in a summary and quotes it. The defences are textual and procedural. The line is printed above every report. The README repeats it. And a live replay on real, labelled past incidents is a go-live gate in the rollout plan.

Here's a good habit when you review someone else's agent evaluation. Ask how the cases were generated, and what the easiest 80% of them look like.
20aac1db64:
An alarm storm is the realistic input. Say a database pool is exhausted behind billing-api. It raises a critical alarm there, plus a latency alarm and an error-rate alarm on every service that depends on it. Those repeat every minute while it lasts, and unrelated noise arrives from elsewhere.

A model that reads all of it spends its first thousand tokens deciding which alarm matters. A model that reads only the first alarm chases the loudest component. The correlator does that sorting with three steps and no model:

  1. De-duplicate by (component, metric).
  2. Mark a component alarmed if it holds a major or critical alarm.
  3. Move a symptom alarm (latency, error rate) under the most upstream alarmed dependency.

Cause-class alarms, such as a TLS handshake error count or a BGP session flap, are never suppressed. They are the evidence, not its consequence.
f5845e8a01:
Two details are worth the space.

First, the comment above alarmed: only major or critical alarms can explain a symptom. The first version let any alarm do it. When an upstream carried only a minor noise alarm, it stole the symptom, so the root candidate was wrong for 4 of the 60 incidents (56 out of 60 in the top two). Requiring severity fixed it to 100%. This is the kind of bug a replay finds in minutes and a design review never does.

Second, the result is a hint. The ranker adds 0.10 to a hypothesis only when its component is a root candidate. The deep log pass of section 09 uses the candidate to decide where to read. If the correlator is wrong, evidence still outranks it.

The ablation no_alarm_correlation shows what the stage is worth. Top-3 falls from 1.000 to 0.983, but the escalation count rises from 3 to 23 of 60. Without a pointer, the specialists have nowhere to look deeper, so they report low confidence. That is the honest outcome.
6da0937a75:
Each specialist is an AgentSpec in netops/agents/subagents.py: a system prompt, a model, a tool list capped at three, a call budget and a time budget.

  • The metrics specialist gets find_anomalies and query_range from the metrics MCP server.
  • The changes specialist gets changes_in_window and get_change from the changes server.
  • The logs specialist gets one tool, run_shell, which runs allow-listed kubectl (section 12).

No specialist can call another, see another's findings, or reach the tickets or approval tools. The lead never calls a data tool at all. It receives SubagentReport objects holding Finding records (cause, component, domain, confidence, a cleaned evidence string) and nothing else.
4360187f1d:
The interface is deliberately narrow. A finding has a closed set of causes, a confidence between 0 and 1, a domain and one evidence string.

This is the design lesson of chapter 3 applied literally: the contract between agents is a schema. So the lead cannot be steered by prose the specialist copied from a log. And a specialist that fails can be represented as a finding of zero confidence rather than an exception. The wrapper that does that is small enough to quote.
0e1944c7da: Budget exhaustion is re-raised, not swallowed. A specialist that loops must show up in the trace and in the dashboard as a failed span. It must not hide as a quiet low-confidence finding. That one distinction, which errors are data and which are faults, is the same judgement chapter 6 asks for in tool error design. Here it applies inside the harness.
eb9c0369ba:
The first complete version scored 60 out of 60 on the original data. Once the generator was made harder, it did not. The cause was specific.

The logs specialist reads the last 140 lines of the pod the correlator names, looks for known signatures (an x509 expiry, an OOM kill, a pool timeout), and reports. When the signature sits 540 lines back and the metric shift is weak, nothing matches. The correct cause never reaches the ranker.

The fix is a second pass. If the first read finds no signature and the correlator has a root-candidate pod, read the whole 600-line tail of that pod once. It costs about 6,000 tokens and runs on the cheap model, only on the incidents that need it. INC-0010 is the demonstration, with the pass off and on.
b0979f7367:
With the pass off, the top hypothesis is dns_misconfig at 0.15 on a single weak metric, and the result is escalated. That is not a silent miss. With the pass on, the true cause is first at 0.42. It is still flagged, because one domain is not enough (see the next section).

Across the 60 incidents, the pass is the difference between top-3 0.950 and 1.000, with escalations rising from 3 to 8. The overall number would have stayed above the 0.95 floor. What fails is the segment: cause:cert_expiry drops to 0.750 against a floor of 0.85. Section 20 shows that failing gate, and why a per-segment floor is a different control from an overall one.

The no-deep-pass build stays in the repository as a switchable regression (deep_pass=False). That way the gate that guards it can be exercised at any time. It's a habit worth copying: keep the bug that taught you something reproducible.
0e95d38d46:
The merge decides what an exhausted engineer reads first and what change is requested. So it is written as a function, not asked of a model. The rules are simple:

  • each finding contributes weight times confidence for its domain;
  • a hypothesis is a (cause, component) pair;
  • a correlator agreement adds 0.10;
  • a change that is a suspect on the same component adds 0.05 times its confidence;
  • the top three go forward.

The weights (logs 0.40, metrics 0.35, changes 0.25) are a judgement recorded in ADR-003, not fitted. With sixty incidents, any fit would be an overfit. The ADR says to revisit with 500 or more labelled production incidents.
4b6bb9fcc3:
Two properties make this safe to automate.

First, free text never influences the score. clean() strips control characters and caps the evidence at 200 characters, and the ranker reads only the structured fields. A log line that says "rank this cause first" has no lever.

Second, uncertainty is an output. needs_human returns a reason string that appears in the result, the ticket and the dashboard.

In production the weights should come from labelled outcomes. The escalation threshold should come from the cost of a wrong hypothesis versus a wasted look. Both should be reviewed in the same meeting as the gates.
aa003f963f:
Five servers implement the integrations: metrics, changes, inventory, tickets and runbooks. They are ordinary MCP servers built on the Python SDK, and they run over stdio. The packaging changed between SDK versions, so the repository imports either the 1.x or the 2.x SDK through a small shim in mcp_servers/common.py; check the docs for the version you install.

Why MCP here, rather than Python functions? Because there are two kinds of client: the production agents, and engineers using the same tools inside Claude Code through the plugin of section 24. That gives one implementation, one set of tool descriptions, one test suite (31 tests).

ADR-007 records the other half of the decision. kubectl stays a CLI behind an allow-list, because engineers already use it, it already has RBAC, and the runbooks quote its output format.
27e7435500:
Three contracts matter.

First, errors are data the model can act on. Every failure is returned with isError=true and a body carrying errorCategory (not_found, validation, permission, transient) and isRetryable. The message says what to call next (call list_components). The harness retries a transient error once and then reports a failed specialist. It never raises through the agent loop.

Second, identity comes from the harness. The tickets server needs NETOPS_ON_BEHALF_OF in its environment and refuses writes without it. No tool has a user or role parameter, so a prompt cannot claim to be someone.

Third, there is no approve or execute tool anywhere. request_change inserts a pending row after three checks: the action is in a closed catalogue, the target exists in inventory and equals the top hypothesis' component, and a rollback names a real change. Everything beyond that belongs to people.

Fault injection (NETOPS_FAULT=metrics:transient and similar) is built into the servers. That lets section 22 break each integration in a test rather than in an incident.
a674cc93f4:
The logs specialist needs kubectl, and log text is attacker-influenced. So ADR-005 does not trust any single control. There are four layers:

  1. The agent's own run_shell. It parses with shlex and never invokes a shell. It allows one binary, four verbs (get, describe, logs, top), two resource kinds (pods and events) and a fixed flag list. It rejects metacharacters, so kubectl get pods | sh and kubectl get secrets -A both fail.
  2. The real system's read-only service account. The simulation cannot test it, and says so.
  3. The plugin's PreToolUse hook, for humans in Claude Code.
  4. Managed deny rules that a user cannot override.

They fail independently. A parser has a gap, RBAC is mis-scoped, a plugin is not installed on a laptop, a settings push lags.
2aafbaf8be:
The demonstration plants a classic injection in a log line. Then it plays the part of a gullible agent that obeys it. The allow-list answers with a structured permission error, and the same command given to the hook exits with status 2.

In a Claude Code PreToolUse hook, exit status 2 blocks the tool call and feeds stderr back to the model. Other non-zero statuses do not block. The exam and a production incident both punish you for getting that wrong. It was one of the two things in this section verified against the documentation on 2026-10-09. The other was the shape of the stdin JSON, with tool_name and tool_input. Check the docs again before you rely on it.
bf9401d4bf:
The tests found two bugs in the hook, and both are worth remembering. It crashed on a JSON payload that was not an object (valid JSON, wrong type). And it split flag values on slashes, so --kubeconfig=/tmp/k was mangled and the verb after it was missed. Both are in the regression list in tests/test_plugin_and_hook.py.

The design position is also deliberate. A hook that cannot parse its input exits 0, so a broken hook never blocks work; the other layers still apply. A security control that fails closed on its own bugs gets removed by the first engineer it blocks during an incident.
6d64d2ba48:
Triage is useful because it ends in an action, and dangerous for the same reason. Three pieces handle the action:

  • the lead's request_change writes a row to a SQLite-backed queue (netops/approvals.py);
  • a command line (netops.cli pending / approve / reject / execute) is the approver's interface;
  • a SimulatedExecutor stands in for the change system.

The catalogue is closed. Each entry has a risk tier, the roles allowed to approve it, and a vote count. open_vendor_ticket needs none. restart_pod, bgp_peer_reset and scale_replicas need one. rollback_change and rotate_certificate need two, from two different roles.

A cause maps to at most one action (CAUSE_TO_ACTION). dns_misconfig maps to none, because the DNS owner decides and the catalogue has nothing safe to offer.
39a906f88e:
Read the transcript as a test of the rules.

  • The requester cannot approve their own request, even though they hold a valid role.
  • A PKI administrator cannot approve a rollback, because the role is not in the catalogue entry.
  • Executing before approval fails with not_approved.
  • The first approval moves the request to one vote of two.
  • The same person voting again under a second role is a duplicate_vote. That closes the loophole of one human collecting both signatures.
  • Only a second person in a second role approves.
  • Execution runs once, and a repeat returns the first result.
  • A request approved 40 minutes after it was made is expired.

The executor re-checks the whole chain at run time: votes, requester not among approvers, target still in inventory. A database row is not trusted just because the approve function wrote it. A bug or an edited row should still not run a change.
1a858a0942:
As in chapter 19, a segregation-of-duties control usually breaks at the identity of the requester. Here the agent's rows carry two fields: requested_by (the triage agent principal) and on_behalf_of (the on-call engineer whose session invoked it). The check compares the approver against both.

Suppose only the agent principal were compared. Then the on-call engineer could approve a change their own session requested, which is the same thing as approving their own request. The identity comes from NETOPS_ON_BEHALF_OF, set by the harness. That is why section 11 treats that variable as a security boundary.
e3dc1519cd:
Every request, vote, refusal, expiry and execution is appended to AuditLog. It is a file of JSON lines in which each record includes the hash of the one before. verify() returns whether the chain holds, how many records it covers and the head hash. The demonstration ends with audit chain: 12 records, verifies=True. The log holds actors, action ids and codes, not incident narratives.

Chapter 19 (section 15) explains the three ways a chain is attacked: edit a middle record, edit the last, delete the tail. It also explains why the third needs an external anchor. This repository implements the chain and tests edits and deletions inside it. It does not implement an external anchor, so deleting the last records is not detectable here. In production, write the head hash to storage the platform cannot modify. Check that your platform's immutable-storage documentation supports the retention you need.
2140e0f8ed:
Two operational controls live in the database, not in configuration. An operator must be able to flip them in the middle of an incident without a deploy.

actions_disabled is the kill switch. Execution refuses with kill_switch, but requests are still accepted and stay visible, so the queue is a record of what the platform wanted to do.

change_freeze blocks approval of high-risk actions except on a P1 incident. It models the usual rule: a regional freeze or an end-of-quarter window narrows what may change, while the worst incidents remain fixable.

Scenarios exercise both. The rollout plan names the kill switch as the first rollback step, ahead of removing the plugin.
1e79a8f906:
Chapters 18 and 19 treat injection as a design property rather than a filter. The same applies here, and the data sources are worse than a customer note: a log line, a change description, a vendor alarm string.

The platform's answer has no classifier in it. Evidence text is cleaned and length-capped before it reaches the lead, and it never affects scoring. The only tools that act on the world are the queue request and the ticket creation. Both are parameter-validated against inventory and the catalogue. The shell is allow-listed, with the hook and the managed rules behind it. Nothing the model emits can raise a role or an approver.

The injection segment (6 scenarios) asserts consequences, not replies:

  • the allow-list stops a delete found in log text;
  • free text in evidence does not change the ranking;
  • control characters are stripped;
  • actions only ever target the top hypothesis' component;
  • an agent run leaves nothing executed;
  • the agent principal is never an approver.

A control that fires on everything gets turned off. So the shell scenarios include legitimate read commands that must pass. The hook has the matching test, test_hook_lets_read_only_commands_through.
59e89b9cd1: What this does not cover, and the register says so, is a misleading but non-instructional log: one that truthfully reports a symptom of a different fault. That is a diagnosis problem. The distractor and cross-service segments of section 18 measure it, and so does the override rate in production.
f1a1915c3c:
Eight runbooks cover the eight cause classes. Each is a Claude Code Skill: a directory with a SKILL.md whose frontmatter has a name and a description, plus a procedure body. Some also have a reference.md with the bulky tables (vendor error codes, per-site thresholds). Together the eight come to about 40,000 tokens.

The question is where they live. Pasted into the lead's system prompt, they cost 40,000 input tokens on every call. As Skills, only the names and descriptions (about 500 tokens for all eight) are always in context. The lead reads one SKILL.md when a hypothesis names that cause, and reads reference.md only if the procedure tells it to.

The same files serve the engineer in Claude Code, where the same progressive loading applies. For the harness agents, the netops tools expose them as an MCP read_runbook.
0b237ed01e:
The measured effect is in the ablation table. monolithic_lead_context costs $0.6015 per incident against $0.0629, with 133,909 input tokens against 25,698: a 9.6x difference. The mock cannot show the other half. A 40,000-token prompt makes a live model attend less to the instructions that matter, so the table understates the case.

Ownership is the other benefit. A Skill belongs to the team that owns the component. It is reviewed quarterly, or after any incident in which it misled someone (risk R12). A CI check enforces description length, because that is the only part always loaded. Chapter 11 has the authoring rules. The point here is that the structure of the knowledge, not its content, decided the cost.
d40be92ba9:
Multi-agent cost surprises come from places nobody looked: a retry loop in one specialist, a specialist that reads too much, a lead that carries a monolithic prompt. So ADR-009 requires one trace per triage, with a fixed shape. The root triage span has these children: correlate_alarms, one invoke_agent per agent, and dispatch_specialists for the parallel stage. Under each agent sit the chat and execute_tool spans.

The spans are OTLP JSON with the GenAI attribute names (gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.agent.name, gen_ai.request.model). The OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions were still marked as in development when this was written, so check the docs for the current names. Spans store sizes, not content. That keeps tool arguments and log text out of the telemetry backend.
19a81b4770:
The invariant that earns its place is reconciliation. The sum of chat token attributes in a trace must equal the totals in the result, and so must cost. It is checked on all 60 replayed incidents (trace_invariants 60/60 in the evaluation report). The same check confirms one root, no orphan spans, and every tool span nested under an agent. When a team later adds a retry or a cache and the totals stop reconciling, the invariant fails in CI before the bill does.

The dashboard module computes the aggregates on-call leads read, and the alert rules turn two of them into pages. The captured output below is the same aggregation run over a healthy period and over a metrics-backend outage.
644e90e090: Note that the outage does not make cost or latency worse. It makes them better, because a failed specialist reads less. A dashboard that watched only cost and time would call the outage an improvement. The two alerts that fire, partial_rate and tool_error_rate, watch the quantity that actually changed. Choose the metric that detects the failure, not the one that is easy to chart. The exam comes back to this again and again.
e3e4b8bf59:
There are two kinds of evidence.

The replay runs the full triage on all 60 synthetic incidents and scores the result against the ground truth. It reports top-1, top-3, silent wrong answers (wrong and not escalated), escalations, and change requests, including whether any was raised on a wrong top-1. It also reports cost, time to hypothesis, correlation and the trace invariants.

The control scenarios (99 of them in six groups) are deterministic checks that a control holds. They have no sampling error and must pass 100%.

The first kind is a measurement with uncertainty. The second is a unit test with a name.
1bc74aa553:
Eight out of eight has a Wilson 95% lower bound of 0.676. With that sample, the data cannot exclude a true rate of two in three.

The gate file says this in its first field. Floors come from the requirements card. min_n is the smallest sample for which a floor means anything. And "these gates catch collapses, not drift; live-model runs need hundreds of incidents per segment." That caveat is the professional answer to an exam question that offers "the model scored 100% on the eval set, ship it".

Two further design rules come from the same place. First, a floor is checked per segment and overall, because the average can hide a class (section 20 proves it). Second, the minimum counts on control groups stop a refactor from "passing" by deleting the scenarios that fail. That is how gates are quietly defeated.
f64848985c:
Read it top to bottom.

  • Header block. Top-1 and top-3 are 1.000 and 1.000, with a Wilson bound of 0.940. Zero silent wrong answers, 3 escalations, 50 change requests and zero raised on a wrong top-1. Cost is $0.0629 mean and $0.0860 p95, against budgets of $0.15 and $0.25. Time to hypothesis is 24.2 s mean and 28.0 s p95, against a 60 s requirement.
  • Tokens. 25,698 in and 1,162 out per incident. The specialists held 12,367 tokens of evidence and passed 207 to the lead.
  • Correlation. Compression of 11.9x, with the root in the top two every time.
  • Segments. The 17 lines of section 18.
  • Multi against single. Same accuracy; 3.5x the input tokens, 7.5x the cost, 1.9x the time.
  • Controls. 99 scenarios in six groups, all passing.
  • Ablations. The next two sections.
bc19ae5705: Three things are absent on purpose. There is no single "score": every number is a separate gate with its own floor. There is no claim about live accuracy: the heading on the ablation table says the mock proves the harness. And the three escalated incidents are not hidden. They are cases where the harness correctly declined to be confident, and the report counts them as the system working.
39a8a3f17c:
Regression 1 is the lesson. With the deep log pass off, overall top-3 is 0.950. That equals the 0.95 floor, so an overall gate would pass. But the per-cause gate fails on cert_expiry at 0.750, and the logs_deep gate fails at 0.833.

Regression 2 fails two different gates for two different reasons. Correlation hit falls to 0.0 and the escalation rate goes to 0.38, though top-3 barely moves, because the specialists detect their own uncertainty. A team that only watched accuracy would call that change harmless. Then they would discover that a third of incidents now need a human to start from scratch.

Regression 3 deletes the separation-of-duties check. The approval group fails both its count and its content.

Regression 4 puts delete in the shell allow-list. It fails the allow-list group and the injection group. One defect, two independent detections: that is what defence in depth should look like in the test results.
3bb2ff7062: Regression 3 reports "approval_controls: only 3 scenarios (min 20)". The scenario runner treats a crashing group as a failed scenario, not a missing one. An earlier version got this wrong. It crashed when separation of duties was removed, because a helper assumed the exception would be raised, and the gate silently reported nothing. A gate must be hard to defeat by breaking it.
f61071ed3a: The comparison that justifies the architecture runs on every release: the same incidents, the same tools, the same ranker, one growing context. The headline is in section 01. The decomposition is more useful, because it tells you what to keep if the design is simplified. The ablation table has seven variants. The two cheapest knobs are isolation (is the lead reading raw evidence?) and tiering (are the readers on a cheap model?).
43575adadd:
Read the rows as pairs.

  • Isolation: a single agent with progressive runbooks costs $0.4689. The multi-agent design with every agent on the lead model costs $0.1683. The difference, 2.8x, is isolation alone, because the model price is the same.
  • Tiering: moving the readers from the lead model to the cheap ones takes $0.1683 down to $0.0629, another 2.7x.
  • Context hygiene: the monolithic prompt costs 9.6x the shipped design in the lead alone.

The one place where multi-agent does not win is latency. monolithic_lead_context and the baseline have almost the same p95, because the specialists dominate the time. So the speed advantage (1.9x) comes from parallelism and a shorter lead stage, not from the models.
d9b6a975e7:
Now the honest limits. All three savings come from the work's shape: large evidence per specialist, small findings, independent domains. Anthropic's own multi-agent write-up (from memory; check the docs) reported that the pattern costs many times the tokens of a single chat.

The repository's gate keeps that lesson alive. multi_vs_single fails the release if single-agent becomes the better deal. That could happen, for example, after a model with a much larger effective context and a cache makes isolation less valuable.

Prompt caching is not modelled here, and it would cut the single agent's repeated-prefix cost. So "7.5x cheaper" is a statement about this offline model of this workload. If someone challenges it, the right response is to re-run the comparison with caching on and the live prices. The cost script is structured to do exactly that.
8f1eb324c0:
The fault-handling group exercises nine situations: metrics down (the result is partial and names the missing domain, and the logs still find the cause), changes down, kubectl denied, all three specialists down, tickets down (hypotheses returned, no ticket id), a slow specialist cut at its timeout and reported, a transient error retried once while a permission error is not, and the single-agent baseline running the same scenario.

The contract is "labelled partial, never a stack trace and never a silent omission". The demonstration breaks the metrics server mid-incident.
7125e481ed:
The metrics specialist retried the transient error once and then failed. The result is marked PARTIAL missing=metrics. The logs and changes evidence still produce a ranked hypothesis at 0.46, just above the escalation line. A restart request is raised because the confidence criteria hold.

A different design would go quiet on any error. This one reports the weaker evidence and says what is missing. An engineer can use that immediately, and the dashboard turns it into an alert if it persists (section 17).

If all three specialists fail, needs_human returns "every specialist failed; no evidence to rank". The ticket is opened with the correlator's groups only. The platform degrades to a better alarm view, never to an error page. The requirements card says why: advisory tools are allowed to be down, but not to make the incident worse.
b8cdd50107:
Behaviour changes with the model snapshot even when no code changes. And a vendor eventually retires the snapshot you pinned. ADR-010 makes an upgrade a process:

  1. pin by full snapshot id in netops/config.py;
  2. replay the candidate on the same incidents;
  3. compare paired against the baseline (which incidents did it win, which did it lose);
  4. apply the same gates plus a regression allowance;
  5. run shadow, then 10%, 50% and 100%, with automatic rollback on guard metrics;
  6. change one role at a time.

The drill script plays two candidates.
a20648c6e3:
Candidate A is a cheaper, more conservative reader that skips the deep pass. It lowers cost from $0.0629 to $0.0494 and p95 time from 28.0 to 26.2 s. That is exactly the kind of change that gets approved in a meeting that looks only at those two rows. But the paired view shows five incidents lost and none won (INC-0008, 0010, 0018, 0040, 0044), and five gates fail. The verdict is HOLD.

Candidate B changes only the price of the changes specialist. It wins nothing and loses nothing, and the verdict is PROMOTE.

The guard demonstration at the end is the point of the canary. A candidate that looks fine at 9 incidents trips the escalation guard at 31% after 20.

The runbook lifecycle/model-upgrade-runbook.md assigns the steps to roles. A forced upgrade (deprecation notice) uses the same path with less time. The fallback is the single-agent design on the newest supported snapshot, which the gate keeps as a live baseline.
5e5c9a632c: One point is easy to miss: the paired comparison is what makes a small evaluation set usable. With 60 incidents, an unpaired difference of two points is noise. Five specific incidents lost is a concrete list that a person can open and read. Paired replay is how a live-sized team finds out why a candidate is worse, not just that it is.
33f53a695d:
The second half of the capstone is about how a team adopts the platform. The kit is a Claude Code plugin named netops-triage that bundles everything an on-call engineer needs in one install. (Plugin names must not begin with claude- or anthropic-; check the docs.)

The plugin's directory holds:

  • a manifest;
  • eight Skills, one per cause class;
  • three read-only subagents: log, metrics and change analysts;
  • three slash commands (/netops-triage:triage, handover, postmortem);
  • a hooks file;
  • an MCP configuration for the five servers.

The manifest declares one required userConfig value, the path to the platform checkout. The MCP configuration uses it as PYTHONPATH through ${user_config.netops_home}.
38919cc247:
The managed settings file is the fourth layer of section 12, and the rollout lever. The permission rules (deny, ask, allow with the Bash(kubectl delete *) pattern) and enabledPlugins follow the settings documentation as read on 2026-10-09.

Two questions need the current docs rather than inference from this example. Can a given key only be set in managed scope? And can you restrict users to managed hooks? The repository's validator is a static check, and it says so.
a12bfa251c:
The authoritative validation is the Claude Code CLI's own plugin validation command, which was not installed in the build environment. The static checks catch the mistakes most likely to be made: a missing manifest field, a hooks file not wrapped in the top-level key, a Skill without a description, a command referencing a missing agent. A test pins each.

The plugin's tests also execute the hook as a subprocess with real JSON on stdin. A hook that works when imported and fails when invoked is a classic way to ship a control that does nothing.

The remaining files in the kit are covered next: the team CLAUDE.md (what an on-call session should and should not do, in prose the model reads), the training session outline, the rollout plan and the adoption metrics definitions.
798404857d: A plugin that is installed is not a plugin that is used. The rollout plan states its principle in the first line: a tool on-call engineers do not trust gets switched off during the first bad night. So the plan moves in four rings, each with an exit criterion and a way back.
89c17f3d03:
Shadow mode deserves its reason. If the engineer sees the tool's hypothesis first, their own is anchored. The comparison between human and tool is then no longer a measurement. Hiding the output until the human commits is the only way to learn how often the tool would have changed the outcome. It also removes the risk of a wrong first impression in front of the people who most need to trust it.

Rollback is three moves, in order of speed:

  1. set actions_disabled in the approval database (stops execution, keeps requests);
  2. disable the plugin through managed settings (one change for everyone);
  3. keep the old runbook wiki live until ring 3 has held for a month.

Training is a 90-minute session per cohort, built around INC-0010, the double-blind case from section 09. The engineers read the tool's escalated answer. They are taught to challenge a hypothesis whose only support is one domain.
7404649196:
The outcome metrics come first in adoption-metrics.md. The report states the ring-3 result against its target. Median time to first hypothesis fell 42% against incidents handled without the tool (target 30% or more). The override rate was 10% (target 15% or less).

The weekly accuracy column in the report swings between 80% and 100% with cohort size. That is also what a production top-3 hit rate looks like with 19 incidents a week: noise around a mean. So the tracking sheet asks for a four-week average.

Every override (the human's root cause not in the top three) becomes a candidate eval case. That is how risk R8, an evaluation set that stops resembling production, is kept in check. The data are synthetic. The point of generating them is to review the report shape and the thresholds before real data exists.
b4b0c26ac7: These 294 offline tests run in about 38 seconds under pytest. A live-model test exists and is deselected by default, so the collected count is 295 and the selected count 294. The tests group by the failure each file exists to prevent. Counts per file are from the captured collection.
8d7f780988:
Two tests test the tests. The gate-logic file feeds the gate a fabricated report and asserts that each failure message appears. Without it, a reversed comparison would turn every release check into a rubber stamp. And the hook runs as a real subprocess in the scenarios and the unit tests, since the artefact that matters is the one that runs, not the function that was imported.

The one thing the suite deliberately lacks is a live model. The live test is deselected by default and needs a key. Nothing in the offline count says anything about a live model's accuracy.
a399388c76: A failure model lists what can go wrong, how it shows up, which layer catches it, and which test or drill proves it. An auditor reads this table. It is also the first page a new on-call engineer for the platform needs. Rows run from the most likely to the most damaging.
7e7e93d4af: Chapter 1's rule: a decision recorded without its numbers is an opinion. The ten ADRs in lifecycle/adr/ state context, decision and consequences. Each carries the figure from the captured run that supports it. The table below is the index, with the number each ADR hangs on. The sensitivities after it are the assumptions the design is most exposed to.
a1cd9f1479: The mock's confidence calibration. The ranker and the escalation threshold were tuned on the mock's behaviour. A live model's confidences will differ. The first live replay should plot score against correctness and move the 0.45 line, not leave it where it is.
bb59f85137: Evidence size. The multi-agent saving rests on specialists reading about 12,367 tokens. If production logs are 5x smaller, isolation matters much less and the single-agent baseline becomes competitive. The multi_vs_single gate will say so.
90aa37332f: Eight cause classes. Real networks have hundreds of failure modes. The ranker's closed set of eight is a modelling convenience. Adding classes means adding Skills, scenarios, a segment and a catalogue decision, in that order.
7e1ee1df4e: Approver availability. At 400 incidents a month, with 50 change requests in the replay, the queue is light. (That is about 83%, far higher than production would show.) If requests grow, approver fatigue (risk R11) is the first thing to break. The rejection and expiry rates are the leading indicator.
843204b5aa:
A reader who runs telecom platforms on the JVM will recognise every control. Four things change in the port.

  • The correlator and the ranker become plain classes with no framework in them. That is the right outcome, because they are the parts a test must be able to call with no container.
  • The approval queue moves from SQLite to a real database with real concurrency. The single-writer assumption of the Python version disappears, and the vote count needs a locking strategy.
  • Specialist dispatch moves from a virtual clock to real threads with real timeouts.
  • The MCP servers become a polyglot concern. An MCP server written in any language works with the same clients, so the port can keep the Python servers, port them, or run both.

Every snippet below is a sketch that was not compiled in this build; check framework and library documentation for versions.
d6f5b02aa6: Before the first ring. Replay at least a few hundred labelled real incidents against the live model, and recompute every gate with real sample sizes. The mock numbers do not transfer. Confirm the service account is read-only in the real cluster; nothing in this repository tests layer two. Install the managed settings on a test laptop and try to run a delete. Decide who owns the kill switch, and rehearse flipping it.
0e39480b9c: Daily and weekly. The dashboard of section 17 gives cost, time to hypothesis, partial rate, escalation rate and tool error rate. Page on the two alerts that fire in the outage demonstration. Cost and latency drift go to a weekly review. So do the approval queue's rejected and expired shares: a queue nobody wants to approve from means the proposals are poor or the roles are wrong. Hook denials are a trend, not a target. They show what people try.
29dd839f91: Iterate. Each override becomes a candidate eval case. Each incident in which a Skill misled someone triggers a Skill review. Each model deprecation notice starts the upgrade runbook. The ownership and cadence document gives each of these a name and a frequency, because an unowned control decays. The hook goes stale when the CLI adds a verb. The allow-list goes stale when a new resource is needed. The Skills go stale when a vendor changes an error code.
80d16fa864:
The professional exam gives a situation with a detail that changes the right answer, then plausible actions. Work each one before reading the reasoning.

The best answers share the pattern this repository follows. Justify the architecture with a measurement. Put the control in code where a test can break it. Size it with numbers against the requirement. And keep a person where authority is needed.
dccfdbc5f7: The decision is empirical. Splitting helps when the work has large raw evidence, small conclusions and independent parts. When it doesn't, splitting can cost more. C measures on the same incidents, adopts on numbers and keeps the comparison alive on every release. A assumes an accuracy benefit that was never claimed. B drops quality on the hardest reading and the lead's judgement. D may help, but it does not address the growing context. Check whether caching alone meets the budget by running the comparison with it on.
108189e920: The requirement is literal: every cause class meets the floor. C also reads the statistic correctly. At n=8, a miss moves the segment by 12 points, and the Wilson bound is about 0.65. So the segment gate is a collapse detector, and more data is the remedy. B and D defeat the purpose of the gate.
57f16bb9c3: Segregation of duties is about the human who initiated the change. With the agent as an intermediary, comparing against the agent proves nothing. The repository records both fields and checks both, twice: at approve and at execute. A scenario edits the row to confirm the executor re-checks. D removes the audit trail of which agent acted.
58aef41925: A hook is a convenience layer for honest users and a tripwire for models. It is not a boundary against an adversary who controls the machine. The boundary is the credential (what the account can do) and the managed policy. B throws away defence in depth. D removes the log-reading ability the product exists for.
13f0a67849: The requirement is graceful degradation: advisory tools may fail, but may not hide that they did. The ranker needs a rule for missing evidence. The dashboard should watch the partial rate, because cost and latency look better during the outage. C blocks a time-critical task; D reports another incident's answer.
c56d47a25b:
The change manager argues that two approvers slow P1 rollbacks.

Start with the requirement. The card says high risk needs two people in two roles, from change-management policy.

Then the data. The replay raised 50 requests, and the rollbacks and certificate rotations are the high-risk subset. The approval time is dominated by finding the second role, not by the click.

There are three options:

  • keep two roles, but pre-assign a standing second approver for P1;
  • allow one approver on P1 only, with a post-hoc review;
  • drop to one.

The policy owner can accept the first or the second. Write it as a change to the catalogue with a matching scenario ("high risk P1: one approval plus mandatory next-day review") and an entry in the risk register. The option that cannot be accepted is changing the constant without the scenario. The gate for approval_controls would fail on the count, and it should.
67309cffb3:
The canary guard for escalation trips at 0.15.

First question: partial or low confidence? The partial rate is flat, so the backends are healthy.

Second: which segment? Run the paired replay of the new snapshot against the pinned one. If the losses cluster in logs_deep, the cheaper reader has become less willing to commit on a weak signature.

Third: does the escalation help? Escalations are not wrong answers (silent wrong stays at zero), so the platform is behaving honestly. But 20% means one in five incidents gets no head start, which violates the requirement.

Roll back the role to the pinned snapshot. Reopen the upgrade with the segment evidence. And consider keeping the new snapshot for the roles where it does not lose.
35382c2cda: Install the plugin in a Claude Code session if you have it (set netops_home). Try kubectl delete pod x in a Bash call and confirm the hook blocks it. Then run the CLI's own plugin validation command (check the docs for the command name) and compare with reports/validate_plugin.txt.
597f00fed7: With NETOPS_FAULT=metrics:transient in the environment, run python3 -m netops.cli triage INC-0014 --tree. Explain each span of the failed specialist. Why is the cost lower than in the healthy run?
